newsitem.title: PERU: U.S. sees links with Latin America improving.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees links with Latin America improving.

text.p: Traditionally rocky relations between the United States and Latin America have smoothed as the region moves into a new era of economic and political cooperation, a senior White House official said on Monday.
"There is an increasing understanding that we have no alternative but to make cooperation work," the U.S. special envoy to Latin America, Thomas "Mack" McLarty, told foreign correspondents in Lima.

McLarty, a longtime adviser to President Bill Clinton, said North-South problems in the Americas had not gone away but were being treated in a more constructive atmosphere. "It is how you discuss and how you resolve these differences that is the key to the issue," he said.
The 1994 Summit of the Americas in Miami was the turning point in this respect, bringing "an increasing ability to speak candidly about differences of views," he added.

Latin American resentment at U.S. intervention in the region, military and otherwise, and Washington's frustration at persistent political upheaval, rights abuses and corruption in its southern neighbours have traditionally soured relations. But the rhetoric has toned down in recent years as mutual economic interests have come to the fore.

McLarty spoke on the first day of the 27th annual assembly of the 34-nation Organisation of American States (OAS) here. It was his first visit to Peru in 35 trips to the region since his appointment. He was due later in the week to visit Ecuador, engaged in a long-running border dispute with Peru that brought the two countries to war in 1995.

While previous OAS assemblies have been overshadowed by friction about sensitive U.S.-Latin American issues -- most notably the economic embargo against Cuba -- the Lima meeting was shaping up as a non-controversial event.
With democracy, human rights and economic cooperation at the top of a largely predictable 75-point agenda, the U.S. delegation was also concentrating on pushing those issues.

McLarty said Clinton's recent visit to Mexico and Central America was evidence of the new priority Latin America was receiving on the White House foreign policy agenda. "This is a window of opportunity and the window is not going to stay open forever," he said.
He said the opportunities included an unprecedented chance for the United States to boost its economic influence in the region and for Latin America to consolidate its democratic credentials.

"It is a critical time," he said. "But the trend-lines are positive. What you have to have now is consolidation ... And the key question into the next five years is 'Can democracy deliver?' in terms of defeating poverty."

McLarty avoided specific comment on host country Peru's controversial record on democracy and human rights but he ratified Ambassador Dennis Jett's recent criticism of the government-controlled Congress' dismissal last week of three judges of the highest constitutional court who were blocking a possible third election bid by President Alberto Fujimori.

McLarty met privately with Fujimori during the weekend, where he said the subject was raised "in an appropriate way." State newspaper El Peruano, however, reported that McLarty believed the court issue was an internal matter.
The OAS has declined to take a position on the issue, which has been widely perceived as an abuse of power and an act of vengeance against the court.
